display.title: Pesach in Lubavitch: From Likkutei Dibburim, Pesach 5694, Part 1
display.summary_short: A Yiddish reading from the Frierdiker Rebbe's Likkutei Dibburim: life in the small town of Lubavitch before Yom Tov, the power of thought, and the joyful Reb Yisroel.
display.summary_long: Told in Yiddish. A reading of the opening of the Frierdiker Rebbe's Pesach 5694 talk in Likkutei Dibburim. It describes the simple Jews of the small town of Lubavitch: their honesty and contentment, the town's charity societies, and the learning of Ein Yaakov between Mincha and Maariv and Pirkei Avos on Shabbos, which the townspeople discussed in groups on summer Shabbos afternoons. The Frierdiker Rebbe explains that through thought and imagination a person can relive scenes from long ago, as the Baal Shem Tov taught that where a person's will is, there he is. Chassidus calls thought, speech and action the three garments of the soul, and thought is the one most closely joined to it, so a person must guard his thoughts even more than his speech. He recalls how every Yom Tov in Lubavitch had its own preparations and customs, and tells of Reb Yisroel 'the lively one', who at ninety still davened and reviewed Mishnayos with the energy of a young man, saying that a mitzvah without kavanah is like a body without a soul, and that a mitzvah is a command from Hashem that should make a Jew dance with joy.
display.lesson: A mitzvah is a command from Hashem Himself; doing it with feeling and joy gives it life, as a soul gives life to a body.
